## Before we start {.unnumbered}

Make sure you have the following files downloaded from OPAL and placed in your project before the session:

```
intro_to_gis/
├── exercises_code/
│   └── ex_3.qmd
└── data/
    └── raw/
        ├── raster/
        │   ├── night_light_15.nc        <- NEW: download from OPAL
        │   └── sedac_pop_2000.TIFF      <- NEW: download from OPAL
        └── gadm41_ITA_shp/              <- NEW: download from OPAL
            ├── gadm41_ITA_2.shp
            ├── gadm41_ITA_3.shp
            └── ... (all accompanying files)
```

You will also need a `data/tmp/` folder -- create it now if it does not exist. Some outputs from this session will be saved there and reused in later sessions.

```{r setup}
library(pacman)

pacman::p_load(
  ggplot2,
  dplyr,
  sf,
  raster,
  terra,
  ncdf4,
  exactextractr,
  rnaturalearth,
  rnaturalearthdata,
  geodata,
  httr,
  jsonlite,
  readr,
  rvest,
  here,
  tidyr
)

here::i_am("exercises_code/ex_3.qmd")
```

## Where does geo-data come from?

Before loading our raster files, it is worth spending a few minutes on the question you will always face when starting a project: where do I actually find this data, and how do I get it into R without manually downloading and uploading files every time?

### Option 1 -- R packages with built-in data

Best for frequently-used reference datasets and examples.

```{r data-packages}
# Vector: world borders from rnaturalearth
world <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")
plot(world["pop_est"], main = "World population estimate")

# Admin boundaries: geodata::gadm() -- no manual download needed
ita_1 <- geodata::gadm(country = "ITA", level = 1, path = tempdir()) |> st_as_sf()
plot(ita_1["NAME_1"], main = "Italy: Admin Level 1")
```

### Option 2 -- Reading data directly from a URL

Best when data is already hosted online (e.g. a GitHub repository or open data portal).

```{r data-url}
url_csv <- "http://s3.amazonaws.com/assets.datacamp.com/course/importing_data_into_r/swimming_pools.csv"
pools <- read_csv(url_csv)
head(pools)
```

### Option 3 -- APIs

Many data providers (NASA, Copernicus, World Bank) offer APIs. You register, get a key, and download programmatically. Here is an example using the Copernicus climate data store via `ecmwfr`:

```{r data-api, eval=FALSE}
# You would first store your key safely using keyring:
# library(keyring)
# key_set_with_value(service = "cds", username = "your@email.com", password = "YOUR_API_KEY")

library(ecmwfr)

wf_set_key(key = "YOUR_API_KEY")

request <- list(
  dataset_short_name = "reanalysis-era5-single-levels",
  product_type       = "reanalysis",
  variable           = "2m_temperature",
  year               = "2020",
  month              = "01",
  day                = "01",
  time               = "00:00",
  data_format        = "grib",
  download_format    = "unarchived",
  target             = "era5_2m_20200101.grib"
)

era5 <- wf_request(request = request, transfer = TRUE, path = getwd())
```

### Option 4 -- Web scraping with `rvest`

For tables on Wikipedia or structured public websites without an API.

```{r data-scrape}
url  <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal)"
page <- read_html(url)

gdp_table <- page |>
  html_node("table.wikitable") |>
  html_table(fill = TRUE)

head(gdp_table)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Document your sources
Always include a comment in your code with the source URL and the date you downloaded the data. Your future self and any collaborators will thank you.

```r
# Source: NASA SEDAC GPW v4 population density
# Downloaded: 2025-03-01
# URL: https://sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/set/gpw-v4-population-density-rev11
pop <- raster(here("data", "raw", "raster", "sedac_pop_2000.TIFF"))
```
:::

## Opening raster data

We work with two real datasets today:

- **Night-time lights** from NASA (NetCDF format, `.nc`)
- **Population density** from NASA SEDAC (GeoTIFF format, `.tif`)

### Raster file formats

| Format | Extension | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| GeoTIFF | .tif / .tiff | Simplest to work with, most common |
| NetCDF | .nc | Multi-dimensional, common in climate/environmental data |
| GRIB | .grib | Used by meteorological agencies |

When in doubt, try `terra::rast()` -- it handles most formats.

### Night-time lights (NetCDF)

NetCDF files store multiple variables and dimensions. The workflow is: open the file, read the print dump to understand its structure, extract the variable of interest as an array, then convert to a raster.

```{r open-nc}
nl_15 <- nc_open(here("data", "raw", "raster", "night_light_15.nc"))

# Always print first -- this tells you variable names, dimensions, fill values
print(nl_15)

# Extract coordinate vectors
lon <- ncvar_get(nl_15, "Longitude")
lat <- ncvar_get(nl_15, "Latitude", verbose = FALSE)

# Extract the light values -- copy the variable name from the print output
light_array <- ncvar_get(nl_15, "HRFC_COM_FR")
dim(light_array)

# Replace the fill value with proper NA
fillvalue            <- ncatt_get(nl_15, "HRFC_COM_FR", "_FillValue")
light_array[light_array == fillvalue$value] <- NA

nc_close(nl_15)

# Convert to raster
night <- raster(
  t(light_array),
  xmn = min(lon), xmx = max(lon),
  ymn = min(lat), ymx = max(lat),
  crs = CRS("+proj=longlat +ellps=WGS84 +datum=WGS84 +no_defs +towgs84=0,0,0")
)

# Check orientation -- if the map looks flipped, use flip()
plot(night, main = "Night lights -- check orientation")
night <- flip(night, direction = "y")
plot(night, main = "Night lights -- corrected")

# Save to tmp for reuse in later sessions
writeRaster(night, here("data", "tmp", "night_light_world.tiff"), overwrite = TRUE)
```

### Population density (GeoTIFF)

```{r open-tiff}
# GeoTIFF is straightforward -- just raster()
pop <- raster(here("data", "raw", "raster", "sedac_pop_2000.TIFF"))

crs(pop)
plot(pop, main = "World population density 2000")
```

```{r world-reference}
# World borders for reference in plots
world_map <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf")
```

---

## Cropping and masking rasters

### Crop vs mask

- `crop()` cuts the raster to the **bounding box** of a reference object -- fast, but keeps a rectangular extent
- `mask()` sets all cells **outside** the geometry to NA -- cleaner for non-rectangular regions

Best practice: crop first, then mask.

```{r crop-mask}
# Keep only Italy from the world map
ita_map <- world_map |> filter(sovereignt == "Italy")

# Step 1: crop to bounding box
ita_light <- crop(night, ita_map)
ita_pop   <- crop(pop, ita_map)

# Step 2: mask to the actual shape
ita_light_mask <- mask(ita_light, ita_map)
ita_pop_mask   <- mask(ita_pop, ita_map)

plot(ita_light_mask, main = "Night lights -- Italy (masked)")
plot(ita_pop_mask,   main = "Population density -- Italy (masked)")
```

---

## Resampling and resolution

Our two rasters have different resolutions:

```{r check-res}
res(ita_light_mask)  # coarser
res(ita_pop_mask)    # finer
```

To do operations across both rasters, they need to match. `terra::resample()` adjusts one raster to match the resolution and extent of another using interpolation.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Resolution trade-off
Going from fine to coarse (aggregating) loses information but is safe. Going from coarse to fine (disaggregating) creates artificial precision -- it makes the map look smoother but does not add real information.
:::

```{r resample}
# Convert to terra for resampling
ita_light_t <- rast(ita_light_mask)
ita_pop_t   <- rast(ita_pop_mask)

# Resample population to match the resolution of night lights
ita_pop_resampled <- terra::resample(ita_pop_t, ita_light_t, method = "bilinear")

res(ita_pop_resampled)  # should now match ita_light_t

plot(ita_pop_resampled, main = "Population -- resampled to match night lights")
```

### Aggregating to a coarser resolution

```{r aggregate}
# factor = 5 means each new cell covers 5x5 original cells
agg_pop <- aggregate(ita_pop_t, fact = 5, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)
plot(agg_pop, main = "Population -- aggregated (factor 5)")
```

---

## Extracting raster values to vector geometries

The most common workflow in economics: you have a raster (satellite image) and you want one number per administrative unit (district, province, country). The `exactextractr` package does this efficiently and accurately.

### Extract mean night light per Italian NUTS 2

```{r extract-nuts2}
# Load Italian NUTS 2 boundaries
ita_2 <- geodata::gadm(country = "ITA", level = 2, path = tempdir()) |> st_as_sf()

# Crop and mask the night light raster to Italy
ita_night   <- crop(night, ita_2)
ita_night_m <- mask(ita_night, ita_2)

# Extract sum of night light for each polygon
light_values <- exact_extract(ita_night_m, ita_2, "sum")
ita_2$sum_light <- light_values

hist(ita_2$sum_light, main = "Distribution of night light by NUTS 2", xlab = "Sum of light")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = ita_2, aes(fill = sum_light)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(title = "Night light intensity by Italian NUTS 2", fill = "Sum") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## exactextractr vs raster::extract
`exact_extract()` is preferred because it correctly handles cells that are only partially within a polygon by weighting their contribution by the fraction of the cell area covered. This matters especially for small polygons or coarse rasters.

You can extract multiple statistics at once:
```r
exact_extract(raster, polygons, c("sum", "mean", "median"))
```
:::

### Extract values for a buffer around centroids

A common technique in economics is to measure conditions within a certain radius of a location (e.g. distance to a port, population within 50km of a city center).

```{r buffer-extract}
# Italian NUTS 3 (provinces)
ita_3 <- geodata::gadm(country = "ITA", level = 3, path = tempdir()) |> st_as_sf()

# Compute centroids -- st_point_on_surface() ensures the point is inside the polygon
# (st_centroid can fall outside for irregular or island polygons)
ita_centers <- st_point_on_surface(ita_3)

# Example: check the difference for a province with islands
messina <- ita_3 |> filter(NAME_2 == "Messina")
messina_centroid <- st_centroid(messina)
messina_surface  <- st_point_on_surface(messina)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = messina) +
  geom_sf(data = messina_centroid, colour = "red",  size = 2) +
  geom_sf(data = messina_surface,  colour = "blue", size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Messina: centroid (red) vs point on surface (blue)") +
  theme_minimal()

# Create a 2km buffer around each province center
centers_buffer <- st_buffer(ita_centers, dist = 2000)

# Make sure the pop raster and the buffer have the same CRS
ita_pop_fine <- crop(pop, ita_3) |> mask(ita_3)

# Population within 2km of province center
pop_center <- exact_extract(ita_pop_fine, centers_buffer, fun = "sum")
pop_total  <- exact_extract(ita_pop_fine, ita_3,         fun = "sum")

ita_3$pop_center    <- pop_center
ita_3$pop_non_center <- pop_total - pop_center

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = ita_3, aes(fill = pop_center), colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(title = "Population within 2km of province centre") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Exercise 1 -- Crop and mask Germany
Using the population raster (`pop`) and the German Länder shapefile (`deu_1` from Session 2, or reload it):

1. Crop the population raster to Germany.
2. Mask it to the actual country shape.
3. Plot the result.
4. What is the maximum population density value in Germany? Use `cellStats(ita_pop_mask, max)` or `global(rast(pop_deu), max)`.
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
## Exercise 2 -- Night light extraction for Saxony
1. Filter `deu_2` (German Kreise) to keep only Saxony (`NAME_1 == "Sachsen"`).
2. Crop and mask the night lights raster to Saxony.
3. Extract the mean night light for each Kreis using `exact_extract()`.
4. Plot the result as a choropleth map using `scale_fill_viridis_c()`.
5. Which Kreis has the highest night light value? Does it make geographic sense?
:::
